extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate CS/math students (CS103; learners of proof-writing)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing clear, correct, and well-structured undergraduate-level mathematical proofs (as used in an introductory CS/mathematics course). Emphasizes exposition, rigor, formatting, and choosing appropriate proof techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include sufficient detail for a mathematically educated reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs exist to convey a line of reasoning to a reader who does not know why the result is true; include details that would let a mathematically educated reader understand why your result is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid terseness that forces the reader to 'rehydrate' steps. The handout contrasts a very terse Pythagorean-triple proof with expanded versions that show intermediate steps and justify deductions. Provide the necessary algebraic steps or short explanations rather than leaving leaps that a reader must fill in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give guideposts and announce overall structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof should give guideposts to its overall structure (e.g., 'By contradiction; assume...', 'We will prove both directions of implication', 'First, we'll prove that...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Announcing the proof method and the main steps helps readers follow the arc. Examples: explicitly state when you are using contradiction, contrapositive, case analysis, or that you will prove two directions of an iff. This avoids reader confusion about why assumptions are being made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use English to convey structure and notation for facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use mathematical notation to convey facts and English to convey structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write sentences that explain the role of calculations; use notation on separate lines to present computations or equations. This makes the proof readable aloud and clarifies the flow from one fact to the next.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label intermediary results and important equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Give names or numbers to intermediary results and equations so they can be referenced clearly later in the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placing important derived statements on their own lines and labelling them (e.g., (1), (2), (3)) improves clarity, lets the reader jump back easily, and reduces dense inline algebra that is hard to parse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify algebraic steps that require conditions (e.g., dividing by a nonzero)
rubrics_metrics.description: When performing algebraic manipulations that require hypotheses (like dividing by a^2), explicitly note the required condition (e.g., a ≠ 0) and justify it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why the divisor is nonzero (from assumptions such as positivity). The Pythagorean example shows explicitly noting 'a is nonzero' before dividing both sides by a^2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why contradictions are contradictions (connect to definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: When reaching a contradiction, state why the contradictory statement contradicts a known definition or previously proven fact (e.g., 'this would make √2 rational, but √2 is irrational').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't just assert 'which is impossible' — tie the impossible claim back to definitions or prior results. For example, after deducing b/a = √2, remind the reader that expressing √2 as a ratio of integers contradicts its irrationality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid terse symbolic lines and unreadable single-line arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid compressing multiple logical steps into a single line of dense notation or symbolic arrows that are hard to articulate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dense inline expressions like 'If (a,a,b) is a triple, 2a^2 = b^2 ⇒ b/a = √2' are hard to read aloud and force the reader to infer omitted reasoning. Break calculations into sentences and separate displayed equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use whitespace and visual formatting to aid navigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Spread the proof out visually with whitespace and paragraph breaks so readers can pause and refer back easily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitespace, labelled equations, and natural breaks make it easier for the reader to find where they were after thinking or checking earlier steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary sentence structure to improve readability
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid repetitive sentence patterns (e.g., many sentences of the form 'Because X, we have Y'); introduce variety so the prose is easier to read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mix statements of facts, explanations of flow, and explicit transitions. This reduces fatigue and makes the logical structure clearer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'clearly'/'obviously' (don't rely on 'proof by intimidation')
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not justify important claims by saying they are 'clearly' or 'obviously' true; provide a brief justification instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flagging something as 'clearly' often hides a missing argument. The handout shows how 'Clearly, neither a, b, nor c can be zero' should be expanded to explain why these variables must be positive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove both directions for biconditionals (iff statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove A ↔ B you must show (i) A ⇒ B and (ii) B ⇒ A; do not stop after proving only one direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sets-difference example demonstrates a proof that only proved one implication and therefore was incomplete. Announce you'll prove both directions and present each clearly (direct proof, contrapositive, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Check and state domains/properties of variables (positivity, integer vs. natural)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly state the domain and necessary properties of variables (e.g., integers vs. natural numbers, positivity) and use them when needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Errors can arise if you assume, for example, that an exponent yields an integer without ensuring exponents are nonnegative. In the coin/3m+4n example, show why m is a natural number rather than merely an integer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the simplest appropriate proof technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer a direct proof if one suffices; use proof by contradiction or contrapositive only when necessary or natural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction can obscure a simple direct argument (n^2 + n example). After drafting a contradiction proof, see if you can present a cleaner direct proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Announce and structure case analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: When using cases, explicitly announce the cases and handle each in turn with guideposts so the reader knows what is being done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In modular/case proofs (e.g., k mod 3 equals 0,1,2), state the cases up front and present how each yields the desired form; explain why parameters remaining are valid natural numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid logical gaps and incomplete arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure your proof contains no missing logical steps needed to reach the conclusion from the assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sets example illustrates an argument that asserted the conclusion without proving the reverse implication. Carefully check for omissions, especially in multi-part or iff proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain an appropriate level of rigor and justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Be neither too terse nor overly pedantic — provide enough justification for nontrivial steps but avoid belaboring trivialities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The handout contrasts two extremes: insufficient detail that forces readers to fill gaps, and over-explaining trivial facts (e.g., spelling out that 3m + 4·0 = 3m). Aim for the level of justification appropriate to the audience (CS103 assumptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat proofs as essays with a narrative arc
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof should be readable as exposition: it should have an introduction (what you'll prove and how), a body with logical steps and signposts, and a concluding aggregation tying pieces together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start by stating the intent, break the proof into labeled sub-steps if needed, and conclude by summarizing how those pieces yield the theorem. This helps readers follow longer proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about handling edge cases (zero, negatives, non-integer exponents, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Check and handle edge cases that might invalidate steps (e.g., dividing by zero, negative exponents producing non-integers, q ≠ 0 in rational representations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The log_2 3 example highlights checking q ≠ 0; the Frobenius and parity discussions highlight attending to sign/exponent issues. Note and rule out invalid special cases explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using advanced results outside audience scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't appeal to theorems or results the intended audience hasn't seen (e.g., invoke Frobenius coin theorem in an introductory course).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an elegant proof uses advanced machinery unfamiliar to graders or readers, it's inappropriate for the assignment. Stick to techniques and results covered in the course unless explicitly allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference definitions when needed rather than relying on intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: When concluding that a property holds (e.g., a number is rational/irrational), call back to the formal definition to justify the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than saying 'this is impossible', show how a derived equality contradicts the formal definition (e.g., expressing √2 as p/q contradicts its proven irrationality).
